title: Vendor evaluation cheat sheet: dedicated inference terms and negotiation script
body:
Purpose:
This working cheat sheet is intended to give GTM and sales-eng teams a procurement-friendly set of messages, a short vendor-evaluation rubric, and contract language snippets when negotiating dedicated inference capacity deals (SLA + isolation + predictable throughput). Use as a loose script during buyer calls and hand to legal for first-pass language.

Audience:
- Procurement leads and platform architects evaluating dedicated capacity
- Legal and finance reviewers needing clear contract asks
- Sales and solutions engineers running commercial discussions

One-line value to buyer:
Dedicated capacity from Redwood guarantees predictable inference throughput and isolation policies that let you convert performance SLAs into engineering and budget certainty while minimizing operational overhead.

Top buyer problems we address:
- Unpredictable latency and token-level cost under shared endpoints
- Risk of noisy neighbors and cross-tenant contention during peak traffic
- Procurement/finance cannot model monthly spend due to bursty usage
- Security and compliance mandates for tenancy and data controls
- Lack of contractual remediation or credits tied to performance violations

Positioning pillars (short):
1) Measurable throughput guarantees: commit to per-second / per-minute throughput bands with explicit test harness and acceptance criteria.
2) Network and data isolation: single-tenant pools, VPC peering, and KMS support with auditable logs.
3) Predictable economics: committed monthly units + overage pricing cap + clear cost-reconciliation process.
4) Operational playbook: runbooks, canary rollouts, and SRE on-call alignment for high-severity incidents.

How we differ vs typical managed cloud endpoints (competitive bullets):
- We expose routing and batching controls so customers can tune latency vs unit cost (most vendors hide these knobs).
- Automated KV/prefix caching and model quantization profiles are part of the deployment, not an add-on.
- Rollout policies and automatic fallback (to lower-cost/compatible variants) minimize downtime without manual intervention.
- Dedicated pools are matched to workload shape (seq len distribution + warm KV profile) instead of raw GPU counts.

Common buyer objections and suggested responses:
Objection: "We already use shared endpoints with autoscale — why commit?"
Response: "Autoscale masks variability but doesn't give predictable per-minute throughput or contractual remediation. Dedicated capacity lets you forecast latency and spend, and provides isolation during peak events that autoscale can't guarantee when noisy tenants coincide."

Objection: "We don't want to lock into large monthly spend."
Response: "We can structure a blended commitment: a baseline reserved capacity priced competitively plus a bounded overage band and step-down schedule for long tails. This gives predictability while reducing upfront risk."

Objection: "Legal wants simple SLA credits, not complicated operational clauses."
Response: "Start with a short SLA table (latency percentiles, availability, throughput) and reference an operational appendix for the detailed playbook. That keeps the commercial contract concise while preserving technical protections."

Negotiation asks (priority order):
1) Throughput Commitment: X p95 response latency at Y rps for defined agent types, measured on canonical test harness.
2) Isolation Guarantee: single-tenant pool with guaranteed vGPU and scheduling window; no cross-tenant co-tenancy during committed hours.
3) Measurement and Reporting: token-level and route-level telemetry with daily/weekly export; 90-day retention for audit.
4) Credits/Remediation: graduated credits tied to throughput violations (e.g., 10% credit for single incident exceeding window, up to contract cap).
5) Runbook + Pager: on-call escalation path with TTLs for response and remediation.
6) Data Controls: KMS integration, optional on-prem connector, and data deletion/retention language.

Fallbacks we can accept (and how to present them):
- If single-tenant pool is impossible immediately: offer a warmed, logically isolated slice (vnet + scheduler priority) with a roadmap to physical isolation within N months. Present this as a staged migration.
- If buyer can't commit to full months: accept quarterly minimums with monthly reconciliation and a pro-rated discount.

Sample contract snippets (phrase carefully; legal will iterate):
- Throughput Commitment (example):
  "Redwood shall provide a Dedicated Inference Pool capable of supporting up to 1,000 inference requests per minute with a 95th percentile response latency <= 300ms for the Customer's production model as measured by the Redwood canonical test harness. Failures to meet throughput targets will be eligible for Service Credits as set forth below."

- Isolation Guarantee (example):
  "During the Contract Term, Redwood will allocate compute resources to the Customer's Dedicated Inference Pool such that no other Customer workloads are scheduled onto the same tenant slice. Redwood may temporarily schedule maintenance tasks that do not process customer inference requests; Redwood will provide at least 72 hours notice for planned maintenance windows."

- Measurement & Audit (example):
  "Redwood will provide daily telemetry exports containing per-route request counts, latency percentiles, token usage, and error counts for the prior 7 days. Upon Customer request, Redwood shall provide a 90-day telemetry export in CSV format for audit purposes."

- Credits (example):
  "If Redwood fails to meet the Throughput Commitment for two (2) or more consecutive measurement periods, Customer shall be eligible for a Service Credit equal to 5% of the monthly Dedicated Capacity fee per missed period, up to a maximum of 50% for that month."

Evaluation rubric (use during procurement calls):
- Technical fit (0-5): Does their offering support our seq-len/kv-cache shape?
- Isolation clarity (0-5): Physical vs logical isolation and timeline to physical isolation.
- Measurability (0-5): Clear test harness and telemetry exports.
- Commercial predictability (0-5): Commitment types, overage caps, step-downs.
- Support & remediation (0-5): On-call SLAs, runbooks, credit structure.
- Integration friction (0-5): KMS, VPC, on-prem connectors.
(note: 20+ is strong; 10–19 requires negotiation; <10 consider not pursuing)

Quick negotiation script (for AE/SE to use live):
- AE: "Our goal is to give you predictable latency and costs for your production traffic. To do that we propose a small baseline reserved pool sized to your 95th percentile traffic and a bounded overage mechanism. Is procurement ok with a baseline that maps to your p95 so you avoid burst surprises?"
- If procurement asks about credits: "We keep the SLA table short but meaningful — credits for repeated failures and escalation commitments from SRE. We can walk legal through the operational appendix which explains detection windows and mitigations."

Red team notes / risk matrix (honest internal view):
- Risk: buyer expects 100% availability like a simple SLA. Mitigation: educate on availability vs throughput and include graceful fallback policies in the demo (e.g., model variant fallback).
- Risk: finance pushes back on commitment size. Mitigation: offer usage smoothing, phased commits, or a pilot month with defined ramp-down.
- Risk: competitor offers lower headline price without guarantees. Mitigation: emphasize unit economics predictability and remediation language; show TCO model over 12 months.

Demo and procurement artifacts to include with proposal:
- Short 1-page SLA summary (table)
- 1-page runbook excerpt that shows page/timelines for incident severity
- Canonical test harness link and instructions for buyer-run tests
- Cost model spreadsheet with baseline/overage/step-down scenarios

Next steps and owners (internal):
- Create a concise 1-page SLA summary to attach to quotes — owner: Sofia Martinez — due: 2025-11-18
- Update sales playbook with negotiation script and fallback options — owner: Evan Park — due: 2025-11-20
- Draft a legal-friendly operational appendix template for review — owner: Ravi Desai — due: 2025-11-25

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep legal language short in the commercial agreement; push complexity to appendices.
- Prepare two commitment flavors: heavy baseline (enterprise) and phased (mid-market).
- Capture a neutral test harness that buyers can run in their own accounts for measurement faith.

End of cheat sheet.
